title: The magic of a pristine sky
caption: The Milky Way arching over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Milky Way arches over ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT). Three of its four Unit Telescopes sit centred beneath the arch, while the fourth is hidden at the right edge of the frame. Further back on the right stands a smaller instrument, the VLT Survey Telescope (VST).

The sky looks divided: a greenish haze fills the left side and a reddish one the right. Both are airglow, light produced by chemical processes high in Earth's atmosphere, and its colour depends on which atoms or molecules are excited. Airglow is extremely faint and shows up only in the darkest places on Earth, such as the Atacama Desert, since artificial light, even from far away, easily overwhelms it.

For French astrophotographer Julien Looten, the picture carries symbolic weight: it marked the end of the night. Keeping skies this pristine matters for cutting-edge research, and it also lets more people experience the magic of a truly dark night, as Looten did here.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Julien Looten; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Airglow is extremely faint, and a camera gathering light over time can reveal its green and red tints far more readily than the eye.
